title: Value Embodiment Practice
opening: A cue is a prompt or arrangement that may support a chosen action. It is not the value, and it does not prove the action happened. Compare what you intended with what you actually did.

labels.sourceExcerpt: Compare a posture, an environmental object or arrangement, and a way of speaking as cues for expressing the value. Retain the cues that help actual action.
labels.practiceTitle: Try one in a real situation

example.title: A cue can look right and still miss the action
example.context: Suppose you want to listen carefully. Putting your phone out of reach is an environmental cue you could test. But if you spend the conversation rehearsing what you will say next, the phone gesture does not show that you listened.
example.posture: Posture: turning toward the speaker could remind you to attend. Check whether you let them finish and can respond to what they said; the posture alone does not answer that.
example.environment: Object or surroundings: moving the phone away could remove one prompt to check it. Check your attention and response; distance from the phone is not proof of either.
example.speaking: Speaking: asking a brief follow-up could give you a chance to check your understanding. A question can still be mistimed or self-serving, so notice whether it fits what the speaker just said.
example.distinction: A notebook labeled ‘curiosity’ is a symbol, not curious conduct. A note that says ‘ask one question before I close this tab’ could be a cue. Asking, investigating or revising is the action to look for.
example.lesson: Try a cue in context, look at the conduct it was meant to support, and keep it only if it helped in that situation. Another context may need a different cue, or none.
